title: Flight Time by Distance Calculator
description: Turn a distance into a rough flight time with the Flight Time by Distance Calculator — a cruise-speed reference table for planning. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 3,000 km at a representative 850 km/h cruise works out to about 3 hours 32 minutes of still-air flying — before taxi, climb and winds have their say.
quick_answer: The Flight Time by Distance Calculator converts a flight distance into a rough airborne time using a representative cruise speed. Enter the distance and read the still-air estimate — useful for comparing routes and sanity-checking schedules, and deliberately labelled rough because real flights add taxi, climb, descent and weather.

body.t: Two routings with different distances become comparable as times: an extra 500 km is roughly an extra 35 minutes at cruise — the unit travellers actually feel.
If a schedule claims a block time wildly off the distance-implied cruise time, winds, a stop or a slow aircraft explain it — or the itinerary deserves a second look. Distance first from the
Charter quotes, sim flights and 'could we fly there?' questions all start with distance ÷ cruise speed. This tool is that arithmetic, done carefully and labelled honestly.
Fermi-style estimation lessons love this calculation: one division turns a map measurement into a journey length a class can argue about productively.

2,000 km — about New York to Miami scale — at 850 km/h is approx. 2 hours 21 minutes still-air. Published schedules for such legs run longer; the difference is the real world's overhead, itemised in the FAQ.
7,500 km at the same reference speed is approx. 8 hours 49 minutes. Long hauls bend the simple model least in cruise and most at the ends — which is why the estimate is a floor, not a promise.

faq: What cruise speed does the estimate use?
A representative jet cruise of about 850 km/h. Turboprops and short-haul aircraft cruise slower; the tool's figure is a reference for jet routes, which are most distance-to-time questions.
Why is the real flight always longer?
Block time includes taxi-out, climb, descent, approach and taxi-in, plus wind and routing. The still-air cruise figure is the irreducible core; everything else is overhead the schedule honestly adds.
Can headwinds really change it that much?

Yes — a strong jet-stream headwind on a long westbound leg can add an hour against the still-air figure, and the same wind returns the favour eastbound. That asymmetry is normal, not an airline trick.
Should I use this to plan a connection?
No. Connections need published schedules with their buffers. Use this estimate to understand and compare, never to cut a connection fine.
Does it work for driving distances?
The arithmetic is generic, but the speed assumption is a jet's. For road time, the driving tools use network speeds instead — a very different model.
As a still-air cruise figure, exact by construction. As a prediction of a real flight, rough by design — the page labels it that way rather than dress an estimate as a timetable.
Can I enter miles instead of kilometres?
The table shows both scales; the calculator accepts the distance you have. Miles ÷ 528 gives the same reference hours at 850 km/h (528 mph ≈ 850 km/h).
